claim: S1PR1 is abundantly expressed by vascular endothelial cells (ECs).
source: S1PR1, abundantly expressed by vascular endothelial cells (ECs), responds to both circulating and locally-produced S1P to regulate vascular development, endothelial barrier function, vasodilatation and inflammation (Proia and Hla, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Proia and Hla, 2015, indicating established knowledge in the field.

claim: S1PR1 responds to both circulating and locally-produced S1P to regulate vascular development, endothelial barrier function, vasodilatation and inflammation.
source: S1PR1, abundantly expressed by vascular endothelial cells (ECs), responds to both circulating and locally-produced S1P to regulate vascular development, endothelial barrier function, vasodilatation and inflammation (Proia and Hla, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Proia and Hla, 2015.

claim: S1P binding to S1PR1 activates heterotrimeric Gαi/o proteins.
source: S1P binding to S1PR1 activates heterotrimeric Gαi/o proteins, which regulate downstream signaling molecules such as protein kinases, the small GTPase RAC1, and other effector molecules to influence cell behaviors such as shape, migration, adhesion and cell-cell interactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S1PR1 signaling mechanisms.

claim: Gαi/o proteins regulate downstream signaling molecules such as protein kinases, the small GTPase RAC1, and other effector molecules to influence cell behaviors such as shape, migration, adhesion and cell-cell interactions.
source: S1P binding to S1PR1 activates heterotrimeric Gαi/o proteins, which regulate downstream signaling molecules such as protein kinases, the small GTPase RAC1, and other effector molecules to influence cell behaviors such as shape, migration, adhesion and cell-cell interactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about downstream signaling of Gαi/o proteins.

claim: The S1PR1 C-terminal tail gets phosphorylated and binds to ß-arrestin after activation of Gαi/o proteins and RAC1.
source: Subsequent to activation of Gαi/o proteins and RAC1, the S1PR1 C-terminal tail gets phosphorylated and binds to ß-arrestin, leading to receptor desensitization and endocytosis (Liu et al., 1999; Oo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 1999 and Oo et al., 2007.

claim: S1PR1 phosphorylation and ß-arrestin binding leads to receptor desensitization and endocytosis.
source: Subsequent to activation of Gαi/o proteins and RAC1, the S1PR1 C-terminal tail gets phosphorylated and binds to ß-arrestin, leading to receptor desensitization and endocytosis (Liu et al., 1999; Oo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 1999 and Oo et al., 2007.

claim: S1PR1 can be recycled back to the cell surface for subsequent signaling.
source: While S1PR1 can be recycled back to the cell surface for subsequent signaling, sustained receptor internalization brought about by supra-physiological S1P stimulation or functional antagonists that are in therapeutic use leads to recruitment of WWP2 ubiquitin ligase and lysosomal/proteasomal degradation of the receptor (Oo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR recycling, with citation to Oo et al., 2011 for the degradation pathway.

claim: Sustained receptor internalization brought about by supra-physiological S1P stimulation or functional antagonists leads to recruitment of WWP2 ubiquitin ligase and lysosomal/proteasomal degradation of S1PR1.
source: While S1PR1 can be recycled back to the cell surface for subsequent signaling, sustained receptor internalization brought about by supra-physiological S1P stimulation or functional antagonists that are in therapeutic use leads to recruitment of WWP2 ubiquitin ligase and lysosomal/proteasomal degradation of the receptor (Oo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oo et al., 2011.

claim: Deletion of S1pr1 in endothelium results in lethality at embryonic day (E)13.5.
source: Deletion of S1pr1 or Rac1 in endothelium results in lethality at embryonic day (E)13.5 and E9.5, respectively (Allende et al., 2003; Tan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Allende et al., 2003.

claim: Deletion of Rac1 in endothelium results in lethality at embryonic day (E)9.5.
source: Deletion of S1pr1 or Rac1 in endothelium results in lethality at embryonic day (E)13.5 and E9.5, respectively (Allende et al., 2003; Tan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2008.

claim: Mice with germline null alleles for barr1 survive without gross abnormalities.
source: In contrast, mice with germline null alleles for barr1 (Conner et al., 1997) or barr2 (Bohn et al., 1999) survive without gross abnormalities while barr1-/-barr2-/- mice survive to term (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Conner et al., 1997.

claim: Mice with germline null alleles for barr2 survive without gross abnormalities.
source: In contrast, mice with germline null alleles for barr1 (Conner et al., 1997) or barr2 (Bohn et al., 1999) survive without gross abnormalities while barr1-/-barr2-/- mice survive to term (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bohn et al., 1999.

claim: barr1-/-barr2-/- mice survive to term.
source: In contrast, mice with germline null alleles for barr1 (Conner et al., 1997) or barr2 (Bohn et al., 1999) survive without gross abnormalities while barr1-/-barr2-/- mice survive to term (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: S1PR1-GS mice harbor one wild-type S1pr1 allele and one targeted knock-in allele encoding S1PR1-tTA and ß-arrestin-TEV protease fusion proteins separated by an internal ribosome entry sequence.
source: S1PR1-GS mice harbor one wild-type S1pr1 allele and one targeted knock-in allele, which encodes S1PR1-tTA and ß-arrestin-TEV protease fusion proteins separated by an internal ribosome entry sequence (Kono et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kono et al., 2014.

claim: In S1PR1-GS mice, the β-arrestin-TEV fusion protein triggers release of tTA from the C terminus of modified S1PR1 when β-arrestin-TEV and S1PR1-tTA are in close proximity.
source: In S1PR1-GS mice, the β-arrestin-TEV fusion protein triggers release of tTA from the C terminus of modified S1PR1 when β-arrestin-TEV and S1PR1-tTA are in close proximity.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the reporter system.

claim: Free tTA enters the nucleus and activates H2B-GFP reporter gene expression in S1PR1-GS mice.
source: Free tTA enters the nucleus and activates H2B-GFP reporter gene expression.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the reporter system.

claim: S1PR1-GS mouse embryonic fibroblast cells respond to S1P with an EC50 of 43 nM.

claim: The S1PR1 reporter system accurately reports S1PR1 activation.
source: Since S1PR1-GS mouse embryonic fibroblast cells respond to S1P with an EC50 of 43 nM (Kono et al., 2014; Lee et al., 1998), the S1PR1 reporter system accurately reports S1PR1 activation.

source: The in vivo half-life of H2B-GFP protein is ~24 days in hair follicle stem cells (Waghmare et al., 2008).

claim: Inflammatory stimuli (e.g. lipopolysaccharide) induced rapid coupling of S1PR1 to ß-arrestin and GFP expression in endothelium in an S1P-dependent manner.

claim: Mice heterozygous for the S1pr1 knock-in allele (S1pr1ki/+) do not show phenotypic abnormalities.
source: Mice heterozygous for the knock-in allele (S1pr1ki/+) are born at the expected Mendelian frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and do not show phenotypic abnormalities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).

source: However, homozygous mice (S1pr1ki/ki) showed an ~2 fold reduction in circulating lymphocytes and ~2 fold increase in lung vascular leakage of Evans Blue dye suggesting that hypomorphism of the fusion S1pr1 allele in the signaling mouse.

source: However, homozygous mice (S1pr1ki/ki) showed an ~2 fold reduction in circulating lymphocytes and ~2 fold increase in lung vascular leakage of Evans Blue dye suggesting that hypomorphism of the fusion S1pr1 allele in the signaling mouse.

claim: S1PR1 expression in aortic endothelium is relatively uniform.
source: S1PR1 expression in aortic endothelium is relatively uniform (Galvani et al., 2015).

source: However, S1PR1 coupling to ß-arrestin, as reported by H2B-GFP expression in S1PR1-GS mice, exhibits clear differences in specific areas of the aorta.

claim: GFP expression in aortic ECs is dependent on the S1pr1 knock-in allele.
source: For example, thoracic aortae of S1PR1-GS mice show high levels of GFP expression in ECs at intercostal branch points (Galvani et al., 2015) but not in ECs of control (S1pr1+/+) mice harboring only the H2B-GFP reporter allele (Figure 1A), confirming that GFP expression in aortic ECs is dependent on the S1pr1 knock-in allele.
evidence: This is confirmed by comparing S1PR1-GS mice to control mice, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The first 2–3 rows of cells around the circumference of branch point orifices exhibit the greatest GFP expression.
source: The first 2–3 rows of cells around the circumference of branch point orifices exhibit the greatest GFP expression (Figure 1A).

source: Areas of the aorta that are distal (>~10 cells) from branch points, as well as the greater curvature, exhibit relatively low frequencies of GFP+ ECs (Figure 1A).

claim: The greater curvature of the aorta exhibits relatively low frequencies of GFP+ ECs.
source: Areas of the aorta that are distal (>~10 cells) from branch points, as well as the greater curvature, exhibit relatively low frequencies of GFP+ ECs (Figure 1A).

claim: GFP+ mouse aortic ECs (MAECs) are not co-localized with Ki-67, a marker of proliferation.
source: GFP+ mouse aortic ECs (MAECs) are not co-localized with Ki-67, a marker of proliferation, suggesting that these cells are not actively cycling (Figure 1A).

claim: GFP+ MAECs are not actively cycling.
source: GFP+ mouse aortic ECs (MAECs) are not co-localized with Ki-67, a marker of proliferation, suggesting that these cells are not actively cycling (Figure 1A).

claim: ß-arrestin recruitment to S1PR1 is associated with increased vascular leak.

claim: Differential expression analysis identified 1,103 GFPhigh-enriched and 1,042 GFPlow-enriched transcripts (p-value<0.05).
source: Differential expression analysis identified 1,103 GFPhigh-enriched and 1,042 GFPlow-enriched transcripts (p-value<0.05) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; see also Supplementary file 1).

claim: The majority (~90%) of transcripts that are differentially expressed in MAECs from S1PR1-GS mice are not regulated by S1PR1 signaling.
source: Intersection of these two sets of DEGs showed that only 9.5% (204 transcripts) were common (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1), suggesting that the majority (~90%) of transcripts that are differentially expressed in MAECs from S1PR1-GS mice are not regulated by S1PR1 signaling.

claim: S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling correlates with heterogenous EC subtypes in the mouse aorta.

claim: The Cdh5 gene exhibited numerous open chromatin peaks.

source: The ~7 fold higher number of GFPhigh-enriched peaks suggests that GFPhigh MAECs are more 'activated' (elevated number of chromatin remodeling events) and/or are a heterogeneous mixture of EC subtypes.

claim: GFPhigh peaks were enriched with p65-NFκB, AP-1, STAT3, SOX17, COUP-TFII, and NUR77 motifs.

claim: GFPlow peaks showed reduced occurrence of p65-NFκB, AP-1, STAT3, SOX17, COUP-TFII, and NUR77 motifs.

claim: S1pr1 WT peaks were markedly enriched with glucocorticoid response elements (GREs).
source: S1pr1 ECKO peaks were enriched with p65-NFκB motifs, while S1pr1 WT peaks were markedly enriched with glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) and modestly enriched with STAT3, GATA2, ATF1, SOX17 and COUP-TFII motifs (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on HOMER motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: S1pr1 WT peaks were modestly enriched with STAT3, GATA2, ATF1, SOX17 and COUP-TFII motifs.
source: S1pr1 ECKO peaks were enriched with p65-NFκB motifs, while S1pr1 WT peaks were markedly enriched with glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) and modestly enriched with STAT3, GATA2, ATF1, SOX17 and COUP-TFII motifs (Figure 2E and F).

claim: 6 of the nine clusters grouped together in a 'cloud', whereas three clusters formed distinct populations.
source: 6 of the nine clusters grouped together in a 'cloud', whereas three clusters formed distinct populations.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: One cluster was designated VSMC-like as these cells may represent MAECs sorted along with fragments of VSMCs, or 'doublets' of ECs and VSMCs.
source: Therefore, this cluster was designated VSMC-like as these cells may represent MAECs sorted along with fragments of VSMCs, or 'doublets' of ECs and VSMCs.

evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and F.

claim: Among the arterial clusters, aEC1 and aEC2 harbored the greatest numbers of enriched transcripts (Z-score >3) with 411 and 1517, respectively.
source: Among the arterial clusters, aEC1 and aEC2 harbored the greatest numbers of enriched transcripts (Z-score >3) with 411 and 1517, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A; see also Supplementary file 4).

claim: aEC5 exhibited the fewest (77) enriched transcripts.

source: To identify genes that underlie the similarity between LEC, vEC, and aEC1, we identified all transcripts commonly enriched (46 transcripts, Z-score >3) and depleted (92 transcripts, Z-score < −3) in each of these three clusters when individually compared to a pseudo-bulk merge of aEC2-6 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

source: Examples of LEC, vEC, and aEC1 co-enriched transcripts were Itga6, Apold1, Kdr, Fabp4, Robo4, Tcf4, and Adgrf5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).

source: Elevated expression of Vcam1, Icam1, Traf6, Cxcl12 and NFkb1 may suggest that these ECs represent an inflammatory cluster.

claim: NOG and ITGA6 were expressed by GFPhigh MAECs at intercostal branch points.

claim: GFPhigh MAECs comprise the first 2–3 rows of cells around the circumference of branch orifices and include ~20–30 cells in total.
source: These GFPhigh MAECs comprise the first 2–3 rows of cells around the circumference of branch orifices and include ~20–30 cells in total.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining observations.

claim: Cells that are more than 2–3 cells away from branch point orifices did not express NOG or ITGA6.
source: In contrast, cells that are more than 2–3 cells away from branch point orifices did not express NOG or ITGA6 (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: TSP1 staining was excluded from ITGA6-expressing GFPhigh MAECs at branch points.

claim: Non-branch point GFPhigh MAECs expressed TSP1 in a patchy pattern.

evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: VCAM1 staining was low at branch points, while surrounding cells showed heterogeneous levels of immunoreactivity.
source: Similar to TSP1, VCAM1 staining was low at branch points, while surrounding cells showed heterogeneous levels of immunoreactivity (Figure 5H).

claim: The aEC1 population includes MAECs that are anatomically specific to branch points.
source: These data suggest that the aEC1 population includes MAECs that are anatomically specific to branch points, while the aEC2 population is located distally and heterogeneously from branch points but nonetheless exhibits S1PR1/ß-arrestin signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunostaining data showing specific localization of aEC1 markers.

claim: The aEC2 population is located distally and heterogeneously from branch points but exhibits S1PR1/ß-arrestin signaling.
source: These data suggest that the aEC1 population includes MAECs that are anatomically specific to branch points, while the aEC2 population is located distally and heterogeneously from branch points but nonetheless exhibits S1PR1/ß-arrestin signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunostaining data showing TSP1 and VCAM1 expression patterns.

claim: Among aEC1-enriched transcripts, 16 were up-regulated in S1pr1 ECKO MAECs, five were down-regulated (including S1pr1) and the remaining 390 were not differentially expressed.
source: Among aEC1-enriched transcripts, 16 were up-regulated in S1pr1 ECKO MAECs, five were down-regulated (including S1pr1) and the remaining 390 were not differentially expressed (Figure 6A; see also Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on comparison of scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The 16 ECKO up-regulated transcripts included positive regulators of angiogenesis (Pgf, Apold1, Itga6, Kdr).
source: The 16 ECKO up-regulated transcripts included positive regulators of angiogenesis (Pgf, Apold1, Itga6, Kdr) (Mirza et al., 2013; Olsson et al., 2006; Primo et al., 2010), regulators of GPCR signaling (Rgs2, Rasgrp3), and Cx3cl1 (Fractalkine), which encodes a potent monocyte chemoattractant (White and Greaves, 2012).
evidence: This is based on data analysis with citations to support the functional roles of these genes.

claim: The majority of transcripts specific to aEC1 do not require S1PR1 signaling for normal levels of expression.
source: Therefore, the majority of transcripts specific to aEC1 do not appear to require S1PR1 signaling for normal levels of expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most aEC1-enriched transcripts are not differentially expressed in S1pr1 ECKO.

claim: Protein levels of the aEC1 marker ITGA6 were not markedly affected at branch point orifices in S1pr1 ECKO animals.
source: For example, protein levels of the aEC1 marker ITGA6 were not markedly affected at branch point orifices in S1pr1 ECKO animals (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: S1PR1 signaling is required for normal expression of some, but not the majority, of transcripts enriched in aEC1 cells located at orifices of intercostal branch points.
source: Nonetheless, these data suggest that S1PR1 signaling is required for normal expression of some, but not the majority, of transcripts enriched in aEC1 cells located at orifices of intercostal branch points.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of aEC1-enriched transcripts in S1pr1 ECKO.

claim: Mice deficient in plasma S1P (Cre+) had ~7 fold fewer non-branch point GFP+ ECs.
source: Cre+ mice had ~7 fold fewer non-branch point GFP+ ECs (Figure 6E and F), suggesting that S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in aEC2 cells is ligand-dependent.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in aEC2 cells is ligand-dependent.
source: Cre+ mice had ~7 fold fewer non-branch point GFP+ ECs (Figure 6E and F), suggesting that S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in aEC2 cells is ligand-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in GFP+ cells upon S1P depletion.

claim: The number of branch point GFP+ EC was not significantly different between Cre+ and Cre- animals.
source: In contrast, the number of branch point GFP+ EC was not significantly different between Cre+ and Cre- animals, suggesting ligand-independent S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in aEC1 population (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in aEC1 population is ligand-independent.
source: In contrast, the number of branch point GFP+ EC was not significantly different between Cre+ and Cre- animals, suggesting ligand-independent S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in aEC1 population (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in branch point GFP+ cells upon S1P depletion.

claim: ITGA6 expression at branch point orifices was unaltered in Cre+ mice and is independent of circulatory S1P.
source: Furthermore, ITGA6 expression at branch point orifices was unaltered in Cre+ mice and therefore is independent of circulatory S1P.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The unique transcriptome of aEC1 cells is largely independent of S1P/S1PR1 signaling.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the unique transcriptome of aEC1 cells is largely independent of S1P/S1PR1 signaling while in aEC2 (and perhaps others), ligand-dependent S1PR1 signaling predominates.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of S1P depletion on aEC1 markers and gene expression.

claim: In aEC2 (and perhaps others), ligand-dependent S1PR1 signaling predominates.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the unique transcriptome of aEC1 cells is largely independent of S1P/S1PR1 signaling while in aEC2 (and perhaps others), ligand-dependent S1PR1 signaling predominates.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in non-branch point GFP+ cells upon S1P depletion.

claim: TFs highly enriched (Z-score >7) in aEC1 are Hey1, Nr4a2 (NURR1), Nr4a1 (NUR77), Sox17, Ebf1, and Bcl6b.

evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Lef1 transcripts were detected at significant levels only in aEC1 cells.
source: Lef1 transcripts were detected at significant levels only in aEC1 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

source: Immunostaining of thoracic aorta en face preparations for LEF1 showed nuclear immunoreactivity in GFPhigh ECs at branch point orifices but not in adjacent ECs (Figure 7B).

source: We noted that all LEF1+ cells also exhibited ITGA6 expression, confirming these two proteins as markers of aEC1 cells at branch point orifices (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

source: These data suggest involvement of LEF1, a downstream TF of Wnt/ß-catenin signaling, in regulating gene expression in aEC1 cells.

source: Examination of postnatal day 6 (P6) S1PR1-GS aortae showed that ECs at branch point orifices expressed GFP and ITGA6 in a manner similar to adult S1PR1-GS mice (Figure 7C).

claim: Non-branch point GFP+ EC were less frequent in P6 mice relative to young adults.
source: We noted that non-branch point GFP+ EC were less frequent in P6 mice relative to young adults (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: There was no appreciable difference in non-branch point GFP+ EC frequency between P6 and P12 or between young adult and 15 months.
source: There was no appreciable difference in non-branch point GFP+ EC frequency between P6 and P12 or between young adult and 15 months.
evidence: This is based on quantification data.

source: In contrast, the number of GFP+ EC at branch points was stable from P12 throughout adulthood (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in non-branch point ECs increases with post-natal age.
source: These data suggest that S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in non-branch point ECs increases with post-natal age.

evidence: This is based on analysis of the mouse organogenesis cell atlas database.

source: Thus, aortic endothelium exhibits spatio-temporal regulation of genes such as Itga6 and Thbs1, with expression of aEC1 genes such as Itga6 becoming restricted to branch point orifices over time while expression of aEC2-enriched genes (e.g. Thbs1) increases throughout the aorta intima after P6.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal and spatial expression patterns observed.

claim: A prominent GFPhigh-specific peak in the first intron of Itga6 harbored a LEF1 motif.
source: A prominent GFPhigh-specific peak in the first intron of Itga6 harbored a LEF1 motif (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7I.

evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data analysis.

source: The Nog gene contained SOX17 and NUR77 motifs in upstream GFPhigh-specific peaks (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A.

source: In contrast, open chromatin near the Thbs1 (TSP1) gene lacked SOX17 and LEF1 sites and instead contained three GATA6 sites (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7J.

evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The GFPhigh status of MAECs at branch point orifices, as well as their unique gene expression program, is not dynamic throughout postnatal life.
source: These findings characterize the aortic branch point-specific arterial EC subpopulation designated aEC1. The data strongly suggest that the GFPhigh status of MAECs at branch point orifices, as well as their unique gene expression program, is not dynamic throughout postnatal life.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability of branch point GFP+ cells and marker expression over time.

claim: The gene expression specification of aEC1 cells likely occurs during development in tandem with epigenetic changes (i.e. chromatin accessibility) and is stable throughout adulthood.
source: Rather, the gene expression specification of these cells likely occurs during development in tandem with epigenetic changes (i.e. chromatin accessibility) and is stable throughout adulthood.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental expression patterns and stable chromatin accessibility.

claim: aEC1 cells have a unique anatomical location in postnatal mice and exhibit high S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling.
source: These cells have a unique anatomical location in postnatal mice and exhibit high S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and scRNA-seq data.

claim: The transcriptome of aEC1 cells does not appear to be directly regulated by S1PR1 signaling.
source: The transcriptome of this EC subpopulation does not appear to be directly regulated by S1PR1 signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of S1pr1 deletion on most aEC1-enriched transcripts.

claim: A combination of TFs, such as NUR77, NURR1, SOX17, HEY1, and LEF1, likely regulate cluster-defining transcripts in aEC1 cells.
source: Rather, a combination of TFs, such as NUR77, NURR1, SOX17, HEY1, and LEF1, likely regulate cluster-defining transcripts in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of these TFs in aEC1 and the presence of their binding motifs near aEC1-enriched genes.

claim: Sagittal sections of the S1PR1-GS mouse thoracic aorta revealed that a subset of adventitial LYVE1+ LECs are GFP+ and thus exhibit S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling.
source: Sagittal sections of the S1PR1-GS mouse thoracic aorta revealed that a subset of adventitial LYVE1+ LECs are GFP+ and thus exhibit S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling (Figure 8A).

source: We observed three distinct expression patterns: VEGFR3+LYVE1+GFP+ (orange stars), VEGFR+LYVE1lowGFP+ (cyan stars), and VEGFR3+LYVE1+GFP- (magenta stars).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining observations.

claim: VEGFR3+LYVE1+GFP- areas were associated with blind-ended bulbous structures that bear resemblance to LYVE1+ lymphatic capillaries.
source: We noted that VEGFR3+LYVE1+GFP- areas were associated with blind-ended bulbous structures that bear resemblance to LYVE1+ lymphatic capillaries (Ulvmar and Mäkinen, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from morphological observations, with citation to Ulvmar and Mäkinen, 2016.

claim: VEGFR+LYVE1lowGFP+ structures were morphologically similar to collecting lymphatic vessels.
source: In contrast, VEGFR+LYVE1lowGFP+ structures were morphologically similar to collecting lymphatic vessels, which are also LYVE1low in the mouse ear dermis (Ulvmar and Mäkinen, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from morphological observations, with citation to Ulvmar and Mäkinen, 2016.

claim: GFP+ LECs were observed at high frequency (73%) in ASMA+ structures but not in ASMA- structures (6%) of S1PR1-GS mice.
source: In stark contrast, GFP+ LECs were observed at high frequency (73%) in ASMA+ structures but not in ASMA- structures (6%) of S1PR1-GS mice (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This is based on quantification data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling occurs primarily in collecting lymphatics.
source: This suggests that S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling occurs primarily in collecting lymphatics.
evidence: This is inferred from the high frequency of GFP+ cells in ASMA+ structures.

claim: Mice lacking S1P in lymph (Lyve1-Cre+) exhibited a 10-fold reduction in GFP+ LEC in ASMA+ structures (7%).
source: Mice lacking S1P in lymph (Lyve1-Cre+) exhibited a 10-fold reduction in GFP+ LEC in ASMA+ structures (7%), indicating that the ligand S1P induces S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in collecting lymphatic vessels.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: The ligand S1P induces S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in collecting lymphatic vessels.
source: Mice lacking S1P in lymph (Lyve1-Cre+) exhibited a 10-fold reduction in GFP+ LEC in ASMA+ structures (7%), indicating that the ligand S1P induces S1PR1/ß-arrestin coupling in collecting lymphatic vessels.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in GFP+ cells upon S1P depletion in lymph.

claim: 30% of S1pr1 ECKO up-regulated genes were enriched in the LEC cluster (Z-score >3 versus the remainder of ECs).
source: 30% of up-regulated genes were enriched in the LEC cluster (Z-score >3 versus the remainder of ECs), while only 7% were enriched in vEC and/or aEC1-6 (Figure 9A and Suplementary File 6).
